cues.chapter: A logo that matches after turning
cues.text: A designer spins a square logo and notices that it can look unchanged before completing a full turn. Would every rectangle behave the same way? Today we will investigate rotations and rotational symmetry, using a fixed centre and clear turn directions instead of judging a shape only at rest.
cues.asr_text: A DESIGNER SPINS A SQUARE LOGO AND NOTICES THAT IT CAN LOOK UNCHANGED BEFORE COMPLETING A FULL TURN WOULD EVERY RECTANGLE BEHAVE THE SAME WAY TO DAY WE WILL INVESTIGATE ROTATIONS AND ROTATIONAL SYMMETRY USING A FIXED CENTRE AND CLEAR TURNED DIRECTIONS INSTEAD OF JUDGING A SHAPE ONLY AT REST

cues.text: Today we are learning to describe turns and test rotational symmetry. We will move from objects or hands-on actions to drawings, then connect those drawings with precise mathematical descriptions. Keep paper nearby if you would like to test an idea for yourself. board_events.text: Describe turns and test rotational symmetry.

cues.text: Here are our three success criteria. I can name the centre and turn. I can track corresponding points. I can count matching positions. We will check these ideas in two worked examples, investigate a common mistake and finish with an independent challenge. A good explanation links what you see in the model with the mathematical rule being used.
board: I can name the centre and turn.
cues.asr_text: HERE ARE OUR THREE SUCCESS CRITERIA I CAN NAME THE CENTRE AND TURN I CAN TRACK CORRESPONDING POINTS I CAN COUNT MATCHING POSITIONS WE WILL CHECK THESE IDEAS IN TWO WORKED EXAMPLES INVESTIGATE A COMMON MISTAKE AND FINISH WITH AN INDEPENDENT CHALLENGE A GOOD EXPLANATION LINKS WHAT YOU SEE IN THE MODEL WITH THE MATHEMATICAL RULE BEING USED

board_events.text: I can name the centre and turn.

cues.chapter: Use tracing paper and a pin
cues.text: Trace a simple shape, mark a centre and hold that point still with a pencil tip. Turn the tracing around the centre without sliding it. Every point follows a circular path around the same fixed position. The original outline remains as a reference for comparing the new position.
cues.asr_text: TRACE A SIMPLE SHAPE MARK A CENTRE AND HOLD THAT POINT STILL WITH A PENCIL TIP TURN THE TRACING AROUND THE CENTRE WITHOUT SLIDING IT EVERY POINT FOLLOWS A CIRCULAR PATH AROUND THE SAME FIXED POSITION THE ORIGINAL OUTLINE REMAINS AS A REFERENCE FOR COMPARING THE NEW POSITION

cues.text: A useful rotation instruction names the centre, the size of the turn and its direction. A quarter turn is ninety degrees, a half turn is one hundred and eighty degrees, and a full turn is three hundred and sixty degrees. Clockwise follows the direction of clock hands.
cues.asr_text: A USEFUL ROTATION INSTRUCTION NAMES THE CENTRE THE SIZE OF THE TURN AND ITS DIRECTION A QUARTER TURN IS NINETY DEGREES A HALF TURN IS ONE HUNDRED AND EIGHTY DEGREES AND A FULL TURN IS THREE HUNDRED AND SIXTY DEGREES CLOCKWISE FOLLOWS THE DIRECTION OF CLOCK HANDS

cues.text: During a rotation, each point keeps its own distance from the centre. Different points may have different distances, but every point turns through the same angle. This distinguishes a turn from moving corners independently. Side lengths and angles of the whole shape remain unchanged.
cues.asr_text: DURING A ROTATION EACH POINT KEEPS ITS OWN DISTANCE FROM THE CENTRE DIFFERENT POINTS MAY HAVE DIFFERENT DISTANCES BUT EVERY POINT TURNS THROUGH THE SAME ANGLE THIS DISTINGUISHES A TURN FROM MOVING CORNERS INDEPENDENTLY SIDE LENGTHS AND ANGLES OF THE WHOLE SHAPE REMAIN UNCHANGED

cues.text: The centre is four, four. Point A is at six, four, directly two units to its right. Predict where A lands after a quarter turn anticlockwise. Imagine the radius turning from pointing right to pointing up, while keeping the same two-unit length.
cues.asr_text: THE CENTRE IS FOUR FOUR POINTER IS AT SIX FOUR DIRECTLY TWO UNITS TO ITS RIGHT PREDICT WHERE A LANCE AFTER A QUARTER TURN ANTICLOIC IMAGINE THE RADIUS TURNING FROM POINTING RIGHT TO POINTING UP WHILE KEEPING THE SAME TWO UNIT LENGTH

cues.chapter: Worked example one: a quarter turn
cues.text: The radius turns upward, so A lands at four, six. It remains two units from the centre. The centre itself stays at four, four. Turning the whole shape means using that same quarter turn for every corner, rather than treating A as the new centre for the next point.
cues.asr_text: THE RADIUS TURNS UPWARD SO IT LANDS AT FOUR SIX IT REMAINS TWO UNITS FROM THE CENTRE THE CENTRE ITSELF STAYS AT FOUR FOR TURNING THE WHOLE SHAPE MEANS USING THAT SAME QUARTER TURN FOR EVERY CORNER RATHER THAN TREATING AS THE NEW CENTER FOR THE NEXT POINT

cues.text: Starting again from six, four, a clockwise quarter turn points the radius downward. The image is four, two. Both images are the same distance from the centre, but their positions differ because the turn directions differ. Always include direction when a quarter turn could be interpreted either way.
cues.asr_text: STARTING AGAIN FROM SIX FOUR A CLOCKWISE QUARTER TURN POINTS THE RADIUS DOWNWARD THE IMAGE IS FAR TOO BOTH IMAGES ARE THE SAME DISTANCE FROM THE CENTER BUT THEIR POSITIONS DIFFER BECAUSE THE TURN DIRECTIONS DIFFER ALWAYS INCLUDE DIRECTION WHEN A QUARTER TURN COULD BE INTERPRETED EITHER WAY

cues.chapter: Do not turn around the wrong point
cues.text: A student turns the tracing around one corner after being given the centre of the grid. The new shape may still have the same side lengths, but it is not the requested rotation. Put the pencil back on the named centre and repeat the turn. Location matters as well as angle.
cues.asr_text: A STUDENT TURNS THE TRACING AROUND ONE CORNER AFTER BEING GIVEN THE CENTRE OF THE GRID THE NEW SHAPE MAY STILL HAVE THE SAME SIDE LENGTH BUT IT IS NOT THE REQUESTED ROTATION PUT THE PENCIL BACK ON THE NAME CENTRE AND REPEAT THE TURN LOCATION MATTERS AS WELL AS ANGLE

cues.text: A shape has a matching position when turning it around its centre makes it cover its original outline exactly. We count distinct matches during one full turn, including the final full-turn match. Our convention calls a shape with only that final match order one.
board: Order = matching positions in one full turn
cues.asr_text: A SHAPE HAS A MATCHING POSITION WHEN TURNING IT AROUND ITS CENTRE MAKES IT COVER ITS ORIGINAL OUTLINE EXACTLY WE COUNT DISTINCT MATCHES DURING ONE FULL TURN INCLUDING THE FINAL FULTERN MATCH OUR CONVENTION COOLS A SHAPE WITH ONLY THAT FINAL MATCH OR THE ONE

board_events.text: Order = matching positions in one full turn

cues.text: Imagine turning an unmarked square around its centre. At which quarter-turn stages will the outline cover the original? Count the matching positions during one full turn, but do not count the starting position as an extra match. Prepare to explain each position rather than guess from the number of sides.
cues.asr_text: IMAGINE TURNING AN UNMARKED SQUARE AROUND ITS CENTRE AT WHICH QUARTER TURNED STAGES WILL THE OUTLINE COVER THE ORIGINAL COUNT THE MATCHING POSITIONS DURING ONE FULL TURN BUT DO NOT COUNT THE STARTING POSITION AS AN EXTRA MATCH PREPARE TO EXPLAIN EACH POSITION RATHER THAN GUESS FROM THE NUMBER OF SIDES

cues.text: The square matches after ninety, one hundred and eighty, two hundred and seventy, and three hundred and sixty degrees. That gives rotational symmetry of order four. We count the full-turn match once. Counting both zero degrees and the full turn as separate end positions would incorrectly give five.
cues.asr_text: THE SQUARE MATCHES AFTER NINETY ONE HUNDRED AND EIGHTY TWO HUNDRED AND SEVENTY AND THREE HUNDRED AND SIXTY DEGREES THAT GIVES ROTATIONAL SYMMETRY OF AUDU FOUR WE COUNT THE FULL TURNED MATCH ONCE COUNTING BOTH ZERO DEGREES AND THE FULL TURN AS SEPARATE END POSITIONS WOULD INCORRECTLY GIVE FIVE

cues.text: A non-square rectangle fails to match after a quarter turn because its long direction has become its short direction. It matches after a half turn and after a full turn. There are two matching positions in one full turn, so its rotational symmetry has order two.
cues.asr_text: A NON SQUARE RECTANGLE FAILS TO MARCH AFTER A QUARTER TURN BECAUSE ITS LONG DIRECTION HAS BECOME ITS SHORT DIRECTION IT MATCHES AFTER A HALF TURN AND AFTER A FULL TURN THERE ARE TWO MATCHING POSITIONS IN ONE FULL TURN SO ITS ROTATIONAL SYMMETRY HAS ORDER TO

cues.text: A reflection uses a mirror line and reverses orientation. A rotation uses a centre and a turn direction. A shape may have both kinds of symmetry, but a line of reflection is not a centre of rotation. Name the transformation before explaining what stays the same.
cues.asr_text: A REFLECTION USES A MIRROR LINE AND REVERSES ORIENTATION A ROTATION USES A CENTRE AND A TURN DIRECTION A SHAPE MAY HAVE BOTH KINDS OF SYMMETRY BUT A LINE OF REFLECTION IS NOT A CENTRE OF ROTATION NAME THE TRANSFORMATION BEFORE EXPLAINING WHAT STAYS THE SAME

cues.text: An ordinary uneven shape may only match after one full turn. Under our convention that is order one. Do not assume every shape has a useful smaller matching turn. Tracing the outline and testing a complete revolution gives evidence, while looking at one corner usually does not.
cues.asr_text: AN ORDINARY UNEVEN SHAPE MAY ONLY MATCH AFTER ONE FULL TURN UNDER OUR CONVENTION THAT IS ORDER ONE DO NOT ASSUME EVERY SHAPE HAS A USEFUL SMALLER MATCHING TURN TRACING THE OUTLINE AND TESTING A COMPLETE REVOLUTION GIVES EVIDENCE WHILE LOOKING AT ONE CORNER USUALLY DOES NOT

cues.text: A student says a non-square rectangle has order four because it has four sides. Test that claim with a quarter turn. Will a long horizontal edge cover a short vertical edge? Decide which matching turns are actually supported by the whole outline.
cues.asr_text: A STUDENT SAYS A NON SQUARE RECTANGLE HAS ORDER FOUR BECAUSE IT HAS FOUR SIDES DEST THAT CLAIM WITH A QUARTER TURN WILL A LONG HORIZONTAL EDGE COVER A SHORT VERTICAL EDGE DECIDE WHICH MATCHING TURNS ARE ACTUALLY SUPPORTED BY THE WHOLE OUTLINE

cues.text: The rectangle does not match after a quarter turn, so four sides do not prove order four. The half-turn and full-turn positions do match, giving order two. The order is determined by exact covering positions around a centre, not simply by a count of sides or corners.
board: Non-square rectangle: half turn and full turn
cues.asr_text: THE RECTANGLE DOES NOT MATCH AFTER A QUARTER TURN SO FOUR SIDES DO NOT PROVE ORDERFUL THE HALF TURN AND FULL TURNED POSITIONS TOO MUCH GIVING ORDER TWO THE ORDER IS DETERMINED BY EXACT COVERING POSITIONS AROUND THE CENTRE NOT SIMPLY BY ACCOUNT OF SIDES OR CORNERS
